title: Blitz puff pastry
subtitle: Rough puff made in 30 minutes with no resting schedule
excerpt: Blitz puff (also called blitz pastry or quick puff) is made by cutting large pieces of cold butter directly into flour, adding ice-cold water, and folding three to four times without a structured resting schedule. It gives about 70 percent of the lift of classical puff pastry in a fraction of the time.
sourceNotes: Blitz or rough puff pastry is a well-established home-baking shortcut to classical puff, widely taught in British baking. The method is simpler than classical lamination but still produces visible layering when baked correctly.

recipe.freezeNotes: Wrap in cling film and freeze for up to 3 months. Defrost overnight in the fridge.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Can be refrigerated for 2 days before use.

content.text: Blitz puff replaces the painstaking lamination of classical puff with a faster rubbing-and-folding method. The butter stays in large, visible pieces rather than an even block, which produces irregular but still satisfying layering when baked. It suits sausage rolls, pie lids, rough turnovers, and any recipe where a very precise rise matters less than speed.
250 g plain flour, 200 g cold unsalted butter, 1 tsp salt, 150 ml ice-cold water. The high butter-to-flour ratio is intentional, blitz puff has more butter than shortcrust.
Cut the cold butter into 2 cm cubes and add to the flour and salt. Do not rub in. Toss the butter cubes through the flour until each piece is coated but not broken down.
Add the water a tablespoon at a time, mixing with a palette knife or fork. Stop adding water when the dough just holds together with large streaks of butter still visible.
On a lightly floured surface, roll the dough to a rough rectangle. Fold the far third down and the near third up. Turn 90 degrees. Roll out again. Repeat until you have completed four folds.
Wrap and rest in the fridge for 30 minutes. The pastry is now ready to roll out and use.

At this stage the dough still shows streaks of butter, which is correct. Do not work the butter in further or the resulting pastry will be dense rather than layered. Baked at 210°C (conventional), the layers open and the pastry rises visibly. It will not rise as evenly or as dramatically as classical puff, but for sausage rolls and rustic tarts it is perfectly good.
